entries.gave: Read the Cut and README.md as it stands: its people are accounting colleagues who save invoice lines from Excel and type one command in PowerShell with the client tax rate, writing no Python, and the developer who does the one-time pipx setup on each Windows laptop. This round sharpens N9 so the everyday steps name PowerShell plainly, and keeps N4 with nothing about licensing.
Read readme best-practice.md N1 to N10 with template.md, and refactor-doc best-practice.md N1 to N8, before any change.

Decided: every decision of the Cut taken as it stands; the one point open, where accounting opens PowerShell, settled as typing powershell in the address bar of the folder in File Explorer, so the step names PowerShell and opens it in that folder; nothing asks.

Invoice tools readers know make a PDF, carry the client name, an invoice number and a date, offer currencies and a rate per line; kept from round 1.

Cut: keep the rows, the typed command and every output line; nothing to drop.
The one way: the rate you type for each client turns your saved rows into that client invoice.
Problem today: accounting asks a developer for each invoice at the client rate.
Doubts: are the totals right to the cent; what if a row or rate is wrong; does Excel save the rows as invoicer reads them.
The person raised wrong rows and rates refused with the row named, and the decimal point; both are in the list already.
All three would change whether accounting trusts the invoice, and the walkthrough settles none of them; kept.
Answers: rounding half up to the cent and adding the printed amounts; refusing with the row named; reading semicolons and a decimal point.

README.md Walkthrough steps 5 and 6: accounting opens the folder of lines.csv in File Explorer, types powershell in the address bar, PowerShell opens in that folder, and in PowerShell they type invoicer lines.csv --rate 19. The rest stands, with no License section and no word about licensing.
